passage:
Every morning that December, the CA coaching centre in Ludhiana smelled of heater dust and chai, and every morning Deepak's stomach turned over on the stairs. He told himself it was the cold.
"You okay?" Gurpreet asked on Tuesday, when Deepak stood by the notice board without going in.
"Totally. This is what I want. Papa's firm, the family name, a stable life. Who wouldn't want that?" He said it quickly, the way he said it at every family wedding.
In the lecture, while the teacher went through tax slabs, Deepak drew the hall's ceiling beams in the margin, then a staircase, then a whole building with a courtyard. When the bell rang he tore the page out and binned it before anyone could see.
"It's just nerves," he told Gurpreet on the way out. "Everyone's stomach hurts before audit."

qa.q: What did Deepak draw in the margin during the lecture?
qa.a: The hall's ceiling beams, then a staircase, then a whole building with a courtyard.

qa.q: Why might Deepak insist "This is what I want"?
qa.a: Deepak feels dread each morning, but calling the family plan his own wish keeps the peace and spares him the guilt and fear of disappointing Papa; binning the drawing hides the other wish even from himself.

qa.q: What could help Deepak hear his own wishes?
qa.a: He could notice the pattern honestly, the dread on the stairs and the buildings in the margins, write down what he actually enjoys, and talk it through with a counsellor or someone he trusts.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet read Deepak's quick "Totally"?
qa.a: Gurpreet saw Deepak frozen by the notice board and heard a very fast answer, so Gurpreet may sense something is off without knowing what.

grounding: A student insists he wants the family-approved career while feeling dread every morning and hiding a different wish.

subtype: Checking with someone who will say the hard thing [Response]
passage:
After the Thursday planning meeting at the Hyderabad office, Rashmi caught Sachin by the photocopier. "Five minutes? I need you to be rude to me."
He laughed. "Rude?"
"Honest. I think that meeting went well. I think I'm a good listener. But everyone went very quiet, and I don't fully trust my own opinion of myself. How did I really come across?"
Sachin hesitated, then said it. "You asked for ideas, and then you finished Neelam's sentences three times. By the third time she stopped talking. And you said 'great point' right before saying why it wouldn't work."
Rashmi's ears went pink. She wanted to explain, and didn't. She wrote down: finishes sentences; "great point, but". "Thank you. Will you tell me if I do it again next week?"
"Only if you promise not to sulk."
"I'll sulk quietly," she said, and smiled.

qa.q: How many times did Rashmi finish Neelam's sentences?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Sachin answered?
qa.a: Rashmi felt embarrassed, her ears going pink, and wanted to defend herself, but she chose to listen and write it down instead.

qa.q: Why was asking Sachin a wise move?
qa.a: Rashmi didn't trust her own flattering view, and a trusted colleague could see habits she missed; asking him to flag it next week turns one talk into ongoing feedback. 👍

qa.q: What might it be like for Sachin to be asked this?
qa.a: Sachin hesitated, so criticising a team lead probably felt risky; Rashmi's calm reaction likely left him relieved and more willing to be honest again.

grounding: An adult asks a trusted colleague how she really came across, and his outside view catches what her self-image missed.

subtype: Not studying so failure has an excuse [Actor]
passage:
On the first day back after the Onam holidays, the Class 6 maths test was in second period, and pookalam petals were still stuck to the classroom floor. Vijay leaned back and announced to Rukmini, loud enough for the row behind, "I didn't study at all. Not one page. I was at my cousin's house the whole holiday."
"Not even fractions?" Rukmini asked, her revision book open.
"Why would I? It's just a test."
But his knee was jiggling under the desk, and when the papers came round he held his pencil very tightly.
A week later he got 11 out of 25. "See? I didn't even try," he said quickly. "If I'd tried, I'd have got full marks." Rukmini said nothing. She had seen him gripping that pencil.

qa.q: What mark did Vijay get?
qa.a: He got 11 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Vijay announce that he hadn't studied?
qa.a: Vijay was nervous about the test, with his knee jiggling and his grip tight; not trying meant a low mark could be blamed on the holiday instead of on not being clever.

qa.q: How could a teacher help Vijay?
qa.a: The teacher could praise effort, show Vijay how practising fractions changes his marks bit by bit, and make trying feel safer than having an excuse.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see Vijay's excuse?
qa.a: Rukmini seems unconvinced; having seen him grip the pencil, Rukmini can tell "I didn't even try" is covering nerves.

grounding: A child who fears a maths test boasts that he didn't study, so a poor mark cannot say he isn't clever.

subtype: Staying up late before a big match [Actor]
passage:
Okay, Gurleen, you want the real story of the final? Fine. It was the night before the winter district finals, and I was so scared of that player from Patiala. She beats everyone. So what do I do? Instead of sleeping at ten like Coach said, I play a racing game on my phone till two-thirty. Level after level. Every time I thought about the match, I started another race.
Next morning I'm yawning through warm-up, eyes burning. I lose 21–15, 21–13. And straight away I'm telling everyone, "I was so tired, I barely slept." Like that explained it. Like if I'd slept I'd have won for sure.
But here's what I only admitted to my pillow later. Maybe I stayed up because I was scared, so the excuse would be ready. That's me, Pooja, doing it to myself. And I wasted my one real chance to find out.

qa.q: Until what time did Pooja play the racing game?
qa.a: Till two-thirty.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep starting another race?
qa.a: Pooja was scared of losing to the player from Patiala; each race pushed the fear away, and being tired would later give a ready excuse.

qa.q: What could Pooja try before the next big match?
qa.a: Pooja could keep Coach's ten o'clock bedtime, tell Gurleen or Coach about the fear instead of hiding in the game, and play the match as a real test of what Pooja can do.

qa.q: If you were Gurleen, what would you want to say to Pooja?
qa.a: As Gurleen, I'd want to say that being scared before a final is normal, that the late night was a choice worth changing, and that a rested loss teaches more than an excuse.

grounding: A teenager afraid of losing stays up gaming before a final and blames tiredness, which gives an excuse but hurts the real chance.

subtype: Leaving an assignment for the last night [Actor]
passage:
The week of Vishu, the college hostel in Thrissur emptied out, and Pallavi had nine days for her history paper. She cleaned her cupboard. She helped Ira's family string lights. She watched the temple elephants go past twice.
At eleven on the night before the deadline, she opened a blank document. "I'm writing the whole thing tonight," she told Ira, almost cheerfully. "Whatever I get, it's a one-night paper, so it doesn't count."
She finished at five in the morning, skipped the references, and submitted at 8:58.
Two weeks later it came back with a C and a note: "Good argument in section two. Needed more evidence." Ira read it over her shoulder. "That's actually nice. You could fix that next time." Pallavi folded the sheet in half. "It was a rush job. It says nothing about me." She didn't read the note again.

qa.q: What time did Pallavi submit the paper?
qa.a: At 8:58, after finishing at five in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi sound almost cheerful at eleven the night before?
qa.a: Starting so late gave Pallavi a ready excuse, so any grade couldn't touch her sense of being able; that shielded her from the anxiety of being judged on a full effort.

qa.q: What did the rush cost Pallavi, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: She saved face but skipped the chance to learn from the note about evidence; next time she could start early, draft a section a day, and use the feedback as a guide.

qa.q: How does Ira see the grade?
qa.a: Ira sees the note as useful and encouraging, something to build on rather than a verdict to hide from.

grounding: A student leaves a paper to the last night and calls it a rush job, so the grade says nothing about her ability, and she loses the chance to learn.

passage:
The quarterly review was at eleven, and at nine-thirty Tushar walked into the design studio in Bengaluru with a scarf round his neck. "Throat's gone," he told Vijay. "Also I was up till two on the Mehta files. So, heads up, today might be rough."
Vijay nodded, and then noticed it: the sore throat before the March review, the "crazy week" before the client pitch, the headache before the demo. Every big presentation came with a warning attached.
He didn't say that. He pulled up a chair. "Can I say something? The draft you sent yesterday was strong. If today's a bit rough, nobody will think less of you. We'd much rather see your actual work than a perfect show."
Tushar fiddled with the scarf. "You think it's strong?"
"I do. Walk me through the first three slides?"
At eleven, Tushar presented without mentioning his throat once.

qa.q: What reasons did Tushar give that morning for the day being rough?
qa.a: His throat had gone, and he was up till two on the Mehta files.

qa.q: What did Vijay seem to feel when he noticed the pattern?
qa.a: Vijay seemed concerned rather than irritated; the warnings looked like signs that Tushar was nervous about being judged, so Vijay chose reassurance over calling it out.

qa.q: What made Vijay's response helpful?
qa.a: He didn't accuse Tushar of making excuses; he praised the draft specifically, said a rough result would be welcome, and offered a practice run, which made full effort feel safer.

qa.q: How might Vijay's words have felt to Tushar?
qa.a: Tushar's "You think it's strong?" suggests surprise and relief; hearing his real work valued seemed to make the advance excuses unnecessary.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate always has an illness or overload before big presentations and reassures him that effort and imperfect results are both welcome.

subtype: Trying fully and accepting the result [Response]
passage:
The building next door was being torn down, and from nine to six the jackhammers made Lokesh's flat in Indore shake. The theatre company's audition was in eleven days.
His flatmate Zeenat half expected the usual. "You'll say it was the construction, na?"
"No excuses this time," Lokesh said. "If I go in fully prepared and still don't get it, I'll know what I actually need to work on. That's worth knowing."
So he rehearsed his monologue on the terrace at six every morning before the drills started, recorded himself, and asked Zeenat to time him every evening. The night before, he could barely sleep, and he let himself be scared.
He didn't get the role. The director's note said his diction was excellent and his movement stiff. Lokesh stuck the note on the fridge and signed up for a movement workshop.

qa.q: When did Lokesh rehearse his monologue?
qa.a: On the terrace at six every morning, before the drills started.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel the night before the audition?
qa.a: He was scared and could barely sleep, but he let himself feel the fear instead of reaching for an excuse.

qa.q: What did preparing fully give Lokesh even without the role?
qa.a: An honest result he could use: the note showed his diction was excellent and his movement stiff, so he knew exactly what to work on and signed up for a workshop. 🙂

qa.q: What would have changed if Lokesh had blamed the construction?
qa.a: His pride would have stayed safe but he'd have learned nothing; a rejection would only have meant "the noise", not "work on movement".

grounding: An adult prepares fully for a risky audition despite noise and accepts the rejection as information that shows him what to work on.

passage:
On a rainy monsoon afternoon, most of the daycare children were napping or at the window watching puddles. Nandini sat alone at the low table with a box of crayons. She drew a snail, then rain, then more rain, humming and pressing hard with the blue. Nobody was looking. Ms Mehak glanced over once and went back to folding towels.
Nandini drew for a long time, tongue poking out. Then she put the blue crayon down, looked at her page, nodded, and slid off the chair to play with the blocks. She didn't show it to anyone.

qa.q: What did Nandini draw first?
qa.a: A snail.

qa.q: What does Nandini's humming suggest about her?
qa.a: Nandini seems happy and absorbed; she is drawing because it feels good, not for anyone watching. 😊

qa.q: How could Ms Mehak support this kind of play?
qa.a: By leaving Nandini to it, keeping crayons and paper within reach, and not turning drawing into a task for praise or stickers.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Mehak gave a sticker for every drawing?
qa.a: Nandini might start drawing to get stickers and stop when they stopped, instead of drawing just because it is fun and finishing when she feels done.

grounding: A young child draws for a long time with no audience because it is fun, and stops when she feels finished.

passage:
"Mumma, done! That's book number nine. Nine stars!"
"Nine already, Irawati? The summer holidays only started two weeks ago."
"Two more stars and I get the art set."
"And the big one Nani sent, about the girl who sails to the islands? You were so excited about it."
"That one's too thick. It would take a week. That's only one star for a whole week."
"But you loved the first chapter. You read it under the blanket with a torch."
"...Yeah. But the thin ones are faster, Mumma."
"Hmm. What if we forget about stars for the sailing book?"
"Then why would I read it?"
Alka put down her tea and looked at her daughter for a long moment.

qa.q: What does Irawati get after two more stars?
qa.a: The art set.

qa.q: Why does Irawati now skip the thick sailing book?
qa.a: Irawati is eager for stars, and a thick book earns only one star in a week, so the prize now matters more than the story she once felt excited about.

qa.q: What could Alka try to bring back the joy of reading?
qa.a: Drop the stars for reading, talk together about the stories, and let Irawati pick up the sailing book just for fun, maybe reading the next chapter together.

qa.q: What might Alka be feeling when Irawati asks "Then why would I read it?"
qa.a: Alka seems worried and a little sad, realising the reward has pushed out the love of reading she once saw under the blanket.

grounding: A child who loved reading is given a star for each book and starts choosing only thin ones, as the reward pushes out the joy.

passage:
The coaching institute in Kota didn't close for Diwali; the only sign of the festival was a string of lights over reception. Manoj sat in the third row with a highlighter, marking only what the teacher said would "definitely come". When the physics teacher paused to explain why the sky looks blue, Manoj put his pen down and waited for the part that would be tested.
"Isn't that cool, though?" Akash whispered.
"Is it in the paper?" Manoj asked.
He ranked 14th in the weekly test and sent the screenshot to his father within a minute. The reply came fast: "Good. Aim for top 10."
Three weeks later, in revision class, the teacher asked about a chapter from that very test. Manoj stared at the question. He had got full marks on it. Now he couldn't remember any of it.

qa.q: What rank did Manoj get in the weekly test?
qa.a: 14th.

qa.q: Why did Manoj wait for the part that would be tested?
qa.a: Manoj is anxious about rank and his father's approval, so anything that won't earn marks feels like wasted time, even something interesting.

qa.q: What could help Manoj learn in a way that lasts?
qa.a: Asking "why" now and then, as Akash does, explaining ideas in his own words, and revisiting chapters after tests would help the knowledge stick, not just the score.

qa.q: How does Akash experience the same class?
qa.a: Akash finds the blue-sky explanation "cool" and enjoys it for its own sake, so the class feels interesting to Akash rather than a race for rank.

grounding: A teenager studies only for rank and a parent's approval, crams what will be tested and quickly forgets it.
